titre: The First International Labor Convention Is Born Full of Exceptions
accroche: Adopted in Washington in 1919, the first international labor convention limits the working day to eight hours, but not everywhere or for everyone.
contenu_vulgarise:
Washington, October 29, 1919. For the first time in history, delegates of governments, employers, and workers from several dozen countries gather in an international labor conference, four months after the signing of the Treaty of Versailles, whose Part XIII has just created the International Labour Organization in the name of "social justice." First item on the agenda: the eight-hour day. On November 28, 1919, the conference adopts the very first convention of this organization, which still exists today as Convention No. 1.

## Eight Hours, Forty-Eight Hours, Except

The principle fits in one sentence, in Article 2: in any industrial establishment, working time may not exceed eight hours a day and forty-eight hours a week. The text carefully defines what an industrial establishment is: mines, factories, construction sites, transport of persons or goods.

But the convention does not stop there, and most of its text is then devoted to exceptions. Management staff are excluded. Shift work may exceed the limit if the average calculated over three weeks respects it. An overrun in case of accident or force majeure is tolerated. And above all, five whole articles adapt the rule country by country: in Japan, the limit goes to fifty-seven hours a week, and up to sixty in the raw silk industry; in British India, it climbs to sixty hours; in China, Persia, and Siam, the convention simply does not apply, the question to be reexamined later by the conference.

## A Standard That Declares Itself Universal and Is Not Yet

What these articles tell is less a drafting flaw than a state of the world in 1919: an organization born of the powers that have just won the First World War, where countries negotiate on behalf of territories they administer, and where industrialization itself is judged too uneven from one country to another for a single rule to apply everywhere. The convention enters into force on June 13, 1921, ratified country by country, each at its own pace.

The fact deserves remembering beyond this particular text: a standard can proclaim itself universal in its title, eight hours, forty-eight hours, while reserving most of its text for saying to whom it does not yet apply. The history of international labor law since 1919 is in large part that of the slow reduction of these exceptions.

repere.texte: The 1919 convention on the eight-hour day allows up to fifty-seven hours a week in Japan, sixty hours in the raw silk industry and for workers in British India, and does not apply at all in China, Persia, and Siam.
repere.source: Convention (No. 1) concerning the Hours of Work (Industry), 1919, Articles 9 to 11, International Labour Organization

carte.punch: ILO Convention No. 1 devotes most of its text to saying whom it does not apply to.
carte.idee: In 1919, ILO Convention No. 1 sets the day at eight hours and the week at forty-eight. But most of its text is devoted to exceptions: up to sixty hours in British India, no application in China, Persia, and Siam.

quiz.question: Why does the 1919 ILO convention on the eight-hour day not impose the same rule everywhere in the world?
choix: Because it concerns only countries that ratified the Treaty of Versailles before its signing in June 1919
Because it leaves each government free to apply the eight-hour limit on its territory or not
Because its text provides longer working hours or complete exemptions depending on the country, from Japan to Siam
Because it applies only to establishments employing more than fifty workers, whatever the country
quiz.explication: Articles 9 to 11 of the convention set different rules for several countries: up to fifty-seven hours a week in Japan, sixty in British India, and no application in China, Persia, and Siam. The convention asserts a general principle while largely suspending it in its own text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which establishments are covered by the eight-hour limit set by Convention No. 1?
choix: Industrial establishments only, such as mines, factories, construction sites, and transport
All public and private establishments without distinction of sector
Only textile factories, the sector targeted by the 1919 negotiations
Agricultural establishments and mining operations exclusively
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The convention precisely defines the industrial establishment: mines, factories, construction sites, transport of persons or goods; other sectors fall outside its scope.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which staff does the convention explicitly exclude from the eight-hour limit?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 2 excludes management staff from the limit; shift work and cases of force majeure are subject to separate arrangements, not a total exclusion.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When does Convention No. 1 enter into force?
choix: October 29, 1919, the day the conference opens in Washington
November 28, 1919, the day of its adoption by the conference
June 13, 1921, after ratification country by country
June 28, 1919, the day the Treaty of Versailles is signed
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The convention is adopted on November 28, 1919 but enters into force, after gradual ratification by states, only on June 13, 1921, a year and a half later.
